paragraphs: Alyosha was on his way across the cathedral square to the widow Morozov’s house to see Grushenka, who had sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message begging him to come. Questioning Fenya, Alyosha learned that her mistress had been especially distressed since the day before. In the two months since Mitya’s arrest, Alyosha had called often at the widow Morozov’s house, both because he wanted to and to carry messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya’s arrest, Grushenka had fallen very ill, and she stayed ill for nearly five weeks. For one whole week she was unconscious. She was much changed—thinner and a little sallow, though for the past fortnight she had been well enough to go out. But to Alyosha her face was even more attractive than before, and he liked to meet her eyes when he came in to see her. A look of firmness and intelligent purpose had come into her face. There were signs of an inner change in her, and you could see in her a steadfast, fine and humble determination that nothing could shake. There was a small vertical line between her brows, which gave her charming face a look of concentrated thought, almost austere at first glance. Hardly a trace was left of her old frivolity.

It seemed strange to Alyosha, too, that in spite of the calamity that had fallen on the poor girl—betrothed to a man arrested for a terrible crime almost at the moment of their betrothal—and in spite of her illness and the almost certain sentence hanging over Mitya, Grushenka had not yet lost her youthful cheerfulness. There was a soft light in the once proud eyes, though at times they flashed with the old vindictive fire, when one disturbing thought took hold of her more strongly than ever. The object of that uneasiness was the same as always—Katerina Ivanovna, about whom Grushenka had even raved in her delirium. Alyosha knew she was terribly jealous of her. Yet Katerina Ivanovna had not once visited Mitya in prison, though she could have done it whenever she liked. All this made a hard problem for Alyosha, because he was the only person to whom Grushenka opened her heart and whose advice she was always asking. Sometimes he had nothing to say.

Full of anxiety, he went into her lodging. She was at home. She had come back from seeing Mitya half an hour before, and from the quick way she leapt up from her chair to meet him, he saw that she had been waiting for him with great impatience. A pack of cards, dealt for a game of “fools,” lay on the table. A bed had been made up on the leather sofa on the other side of the room, and Maximov lay half-reclining on it. He wore a dressing-gown and a cotton nightcap, and he was plainly ill and weak, though he was smiling blissfully. When the homeless old man had come back with Grushenka from Mokroe two months before, he had simply stayed on, and he was still staying with her. He had arrived with her in rain and sleet, sat down on the sofa, drenched and scared, and gazed at her in silence with a timid, pleading smile. Grushenka, in terrible grief and in the first stage of fever, almost forgot he existed in all she had to do during the first half-hour after her arrival. Suddenly she happened to look at him intently, and he gave a pitiful, helpless little laugh. She called Fenya and told her to give him something to eat. All that day he sat in the same place, almost without stirring. When it got dark and the shutters were closed, Fenya asked her mistress:
“Is the gentleman going to stay the night, mistress?”
“Yes, make up a bed for him on the sofa,” answered Grushenka.

Questioning him more closely, Grushenka learned that he literally had nowhere to go, and that “Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me straight out that he wouldn’t take me in again, and he gave me five roubles.”

“Well, God bless you, you’d better stay, then,” Grushenka decided in her grief, smiling at him with pity. Her smile wrung the old man’s heart, and his lips twitched with grateful tears. And so the destitute wanderer had stayed with her ever since. He did not leave the house even when she was ill. Fenya and her grandmother, the cook, did not turn him out but went on serving him meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka had grown used to him, and when she came back from seeing Mitya (whom she had begun to visit in prison before she was really well), she would sit down and start talking to “Maximushka” about trifles, to keep from thinking of her sorrow. The old man turned out to be a good storyteller at times, so that in the end she needed him. Grushenka saw hardly anyone but Alyosha, who did not come every day and never stayed long. Her old merchant lay seriously ill at this time, “at his last gasp,” as they said in the town, and he did in fact die a week after Mitya’s trial. Three weeks before his death, feeling the end coming, he finally made his sons, their wives and children come upstairs to him and ordered them never to leave him again. From that moment he gave his servants strict orders not to admit Grushenka and to tell her, if she came, “The master wishes you long life and happiness and tells you to forget him.” But Grushenka sent almost every day to ask how he was.

“You’ve come at last!” she cried, throwing down the cards and greeting Alyosha joyfully. “Maximushka’s been scaring me that perhaps you wouldn’t come. Ah, how I need you! Sit down at the table. What will you have—coffee?”
“Yes, please,” said Alyosha, sitting down at the table. “I’m very hungry.”

“Good. Fenya, Fenya, coffee,” cried Grushenka. “It’s been ready for you a long time. And bring some little pies, and make sure they’re hot. Do you know, we had a storm over those pies today. I took them to the prison for him, and would you believe it, he threw them back at me. He wouldn’t eat them. He flung one of them on the floor and stamped on it. So I said to him, ‘I’ll leave them with the warder. If you don’t eat them before evening, then your venomous spite must be enough for you!’ With that I went away. We quarreled again, would you believe it? Whenever I go, we quarrel.”
Grushenka said all this in one breath, in her agitation. Maximov, feeling nervous, smiled at once and looked at the floor.
“What did you quarrel about this time?” asked Alyosha.

“I didn’t expect it in the least. Just imagine, he’s jealous of the Pole. ‘Why are you keeping him?’ he said. ‘So you’ve started keeping him.’ He’s jealous, jealous of me all the time, jealous when he eats and when he sleeps! Last week he even took it into his head to be jealous of Kuzma.”
“But he knew about the Pole before?”

“Yes, but that’s how it is. He’s known about him from the very beginning, but today he suddenly got up and started scolding about him. I’m ashamed to repeat what he said. Silly fellow! Rakitin went in as I came out. Maybe Rakitin is egging him on. What do you think?” she added carelessly.
“He loves you, that’s what it is. He loves you so much. And now he’s especially worried.”

“I should think he would be, with the trial tomorrow. And I went to him to say something about tomorrow, because I dread to think what will happen then. You say he’s worried, but how worried I am! And he talks about the Pole! He’s too silly! At least he isn’t jealous of Maximushka yet.”
“My wife was dreadfully jealous over me, too,” Maximov put in.
“Jealous of you?” Grushenka laughed in spite of herself. “Who could she have been jealous of?”
“Of the servant girls.”

“Hold your tongue, Maximushka, I’m in no mood for laughing now. I feel angry. Don’t ogle the pies. I won’t give you any, they’re not good for you, and I won’t give you any vodka either. I have to look after him, too, as if I ran an almshouse,” she laughed.
“I don’t deserve your kindness. I’m a worthless creature,” said Maximov, with tears in his voice. “You’d do better to spend your kindness on people more useful than me.”

“Ech, everyone is useful, Maximushka, and how can we tell who’s the most useful? If only that Pole didn’t exist, Alyosha. He’s taken it into his head to fall ill today, too. I’ve been to see him also. And I’ll send him some pies, too, on purpose. I hadn’t sent him any, but Mitya accused me of it, so now I will! Ah, here’s Fenya with a letter! Yes, it’s from the Poles—begging again!”

Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent an extremely long and characteristically eloquent letter, in which he begged her to lend him three roubles. The letter enclosed a receipt for the sum, with a promise to repay it within three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. During the fortnight of her convalescence Grushenka had received many such letters, with such receipts, from her former lover. But she knew that the two Poles had come to ask after her health during her illness. The first letter she got from them was a long one, written on large notepaper, with a big family crest on the seal. It was so obscure and rhetorical that Grushenka put it down before she had read half, unable to make head or tail of it. She couldn’t attend to letters then. The next day another followed the first, in which Pan Mussyalovitch begged her for a loan of two thousand roubles for a very short time. Grushenka left that letter unanswered too. A whole series of letters followed, one every day, all as pompous and rhetorical, but the loan asked for gradually shrank to a hundred roubles, then to twenty-five, to ten, and finally Grushenka received a letter in which both Poles begged her for just one rouble and enclosed a receipt signed by both.

Then Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them, and at dusk she went to their lodging herself. She found the two Poles in great poverty, almost destitute, with no food or fuel, no cigarettes, and in debt to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they had carried off from Mitya at Mokroe had soon disappeared. But Grushenka was surprised that they received her with arrogant dignity and self-assertion, with the greatest formality and pompous speeches. Grushenka simply laughed and gave her former admirer ten roubles. Then, laughing, she told Mitya about it, and he was not in the least jealous. But ever since, the Poles had attached themselves to Grushenka and bombarded her daily with requests for money, and she had always sent them small sums. And now, that very day, Mitya had taken it into his head to be fearfully jealous.

“Like a fool, I went round to him just for a minute, on my way to see Mitya, because he’s ill too, my Pole,” Grushenka began again with nervous haste. “I was laughing, telling Mitya about it. ‘Imagine,’ I said, ‘my Pole had the happy thought of singing his old songs to me, with the guitar. He thought I’d be touched and marry him!’ Mitya leapt up swearing.... So there, I’ll send them the pies! Fenya, is it that little girl they’ve sent? Here, give her three roubles and pack a dozen pies up in a paper and tell her to take them. And you, Alyosha, be sure to tell Mitya that I did send them the pies.”
